title_en: Chen Xueqin v. Chongqing Commerce Group New Century Department Store Chain Operation Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over product seller liability
ruling_gist_en: Although the product labeling method does not comply with regulatory requirements, it does not cause consumers to mistakenly purchase. This falls under the circumstance of 'not conforming to the product standard indicated on the product or its packaging', and shall support the consumer's request for return in accordance with Article 40 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China.

full_text_en:
Chen Xueqin v. Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over liability of product seller

Ruling Summary

Where the labeling method of a product does not comply with regulatory requirements but does not cause consumers to make erroneous purchases, it falls under the circumstance of "not conforming to the product standard indicated on the product or its packaging," and the consumer's request for return of the goods shall be supported in accordance with Article 40 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China.

Plaintiff: Chen Xueqin, female, 34 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Jianyang City, Sichuan Province.

Defendant: Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd., domiciled at Guanyinqiao Pedestrian Street, Jiangbei District, Chongqing.
Legal Representative: Li Yong, General Manager of the Company.

Defendant: Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd., Century Xindu Branch, domiciled at Guanyinqiao Pedestrian Street, Jiangbei District, Chongqing.
Person in Charge: Dai Yuxia, General Manager of the Branch.

The plaintiff, Chen Xueqin, filed an action with the Jiangbei District People's Court of Chongqing against the defendants, Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as New Century Department Store Company) and Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd., Century Xindu Branch (hereinafter referred to as Century Xindu), concerning a dispute over liability of product seller.

Plaintiff's Allegations: On March 17, 2014, the plaintiff purchased 4 boxes of Tianbao brand pure Cordyceps sinensis capsules produced by Chongqing Huiyuan Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huiyuan Company) from the defendant Century Xindu, at a total price of RMB 50,046. The product bore no approval number or product implementation standard, but displayed a drug manufacturing license number and a product quality conformity mark. The license authorizing the product only covered traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces, not pure Cordyceps sinensis capsules. The defendants New Century Department Store Company and Century Xindu committed fraud by selling the product at issue. The plaintiff requested the court to order New Century Department Store Company and Century Xindu to refund the purchase price of RMB 50,046 and pay triple damages of RMB 150,138.

Defendants' Defense: Labeling the drug manufacturing license number on the packaging of the Cordyceps sinensis capsules did not violate any prohibitive provisions of laws or regulations. Ordinary consumers would not mistake the product for a drug simply because it bore a drug manufacturing license number. Moreover, the labeling of product quality conformity was truthful. Therefore, the defendants had no conduct constituting fraud or misleading consumers.

Facts Found by the Court at First Instance (Jiangbei District People's Court of Chongqing):

On March 17, 2014, the plaintiff Chen Xueqin purchased from the defendant Century Xindu 4 boxes of Tianbao brand pure Cordyceps sinensis capsules: 3 boxes at RMB 15,010 per box and 1 box at RMB 5,016 per box, totaling RMB 50,046. The outer packaging of the product indicated: Drug Manufacturing License No. 20100061; Ingredients: pure Cordyceps sinensis powder; Specification: 0.25g/capsule × 60 capsules; Production date: January 3, 2014; Expiration date: July 2, 2015; Manufacturer: Huiyuan Company. The outer packaging also bore the marking "Product Quality Qualified." On May 26, 2014, the Chongqing Municipal Food and Drug Administration issued to the Shapingba Sub-bureau of the Chongqing Municipal Food and Drug Administration the "Reply on the Determination of the Legality of Pure Cordyceps sinensis Capsules," stating that Cordyceps sinensis falls within the category of nourishing and health care Chinese medicinal materials, and the pure Cordyceps sinensis capsules produced by Huiyuan Company are nourishing and health care Chinese medicinal materials; the sale of nourishing and health care Chinese medicinal materials is a general business item under industrial and commercial registration, not a licensed drug operation item.

It was also found that on December 22, 2010, Huiyuan Company obtained a drug manufacturing license from the Chongqing Municipal Food and Drug Administration, numbered Yu 20100061, with the scope of production: traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces (including decoction pieces for direct administration), toxic traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces; the license was valid until December 21, 2015.

Opinion of the Court at First Instance (Jiangbei District People's Court of Chongqing):

The plaintiff Chen Xueqin submitted invoices and physical products as evidence sufficient to establish a sales contract relationship with the defendant Century Xindu. Chen Xueqin claimed that the product at issue sold by Century Xindu fraudulently used a drug manufacturing license number and falsely marked a quality conformity label, causing her to mistakenly believe the product was one that had obtained a drug manufacturing license number and was of qualified quality. She therefore requested a return of goods and triple damages. The Chongqing Municipal Food and Drug Administration issued a drug manufacturing license to Huiyuan Company, with the approved scope of production including traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces and toxic traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces. The license was issued to Huiyuan Company, not specifically for the product at issue. The product at issue is not a traditional Chinese medicine decoction piece, and both parties confirmed that there are no national, local, or industry standards for the product. While labeling the drug manufacturing license number and the quality conformity mark on the outer packaging was indeed inappropriate, the outer packaging also clearly indicated the ingredients as pure Cordyceps sinensis powder, the specification as 0.25g/capsule × 60 capsules, among other information, which would not cause Chen Xueqin to make an erroneous purchase. The parties bear the burden of proving the facts on which their claims are based or that rebut the other party's claims. If there is no evidence, or the evidence is insufficient to prove the factual assertions, the party bearing the burden of proof shall bear the adverse consequences. Chen Xueqin's request for a return of goods and triple damages on the ground that New Century Department Store Company and Century Xindu committed fraud lacked sufficient evidence and was not supported.

Accordingly, the Jiangbei District People's Court of Chongqing, in accordance with Article 5 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 2 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, and Article 142 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment on June 6, 2016:

Rejected all claims of the plaintiff Chen Xueqin.

Chen Xueqin appealed against the first-instance judgment to the Chongqing First Intermediate People's Court, arguing: The drug manufacturing license number indicated on the product at issue (Tianbao brand pure Cordyceps sinensis capsules) was not the product's own manufacturing license number, constituting a fraudulent use of the drug manufacturing license number; the product bore a "quality qualified" label, but the enterprise standard it implemented was not legally filed, and without such filing, the self-labeling of "quality qualified" constituted a false quality conformity mark, amounting to fraud. Therefore, she requested the revocation of the first-instance judgment and a judgment in favor of her first-instance claims.

Appellees' Defense (New Century Department Store Company and Century Xindu): The first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. They requested the appeal be dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

The Chongqing First Intermediate People's Court, on second instance, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

It was also found that Century Xindu is a branch established by New Century Department Store Company and does not have independent legal personality.

Opinion of the Court at Second Instance (Chongqing First Intermediate People's Court):

The issues in dispute are: (1) whether the act of labeling a drug manufacturing license number on the product at issue violates any prohibitive provisions of laws or regulations; (2) whether the merchant constitutes fraud; and (3) the issue of liability.

I. Whether labeling a drug manufacturing license number on the product at issue violates any prohibitive provisions of laws or regulations.

A drug manufacturing license is issued by the drug regulatory authority to a drug manufacturer, and each license has a specific number and corresponding scope of production. The drug manufacturing license number indicated on the product at issue, Yu 20100061, was issued to Huiyuan Company, with the scope of production stated as "production of traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces (including decoction pieces for direct administration), toxic traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces." According to the definition in the Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China, "traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces refer to processed and prepared Chinese medicinal materials that can be directly used for dispensing or formulation." Article 10, paragraph 2 of the Drug Administration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces must be processed in accordance with the national drug standards; where no national drug standards exist, they must be processed in accordance with the processing specifications formulated by the drug regulatory authority of the province, autonomous region, or municipality directly under the Central Government. The processing specifications formulated by such authority shall be filed with the drug regulatory authority of the State Council." Accordingly, traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces are processed from Chinese medicinal materials, but they must be prepared in the prescribed manner and be included in the "traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces" directory of the Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China. Cordyceps sinensis capsules do not meet this requirement, so they cannot be classified as traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces, nor can they bear the manufacturing license number for traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces.

The Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China includes Cordyceps sinensis, which is a Chinese medicinal material, a fact not disputed by the appellant and appellees. Article 55, item (1) of the Quality Management Standard for the Production of Chinese Medicinal Materials (Trial) provides: "Chinese medicinal materials refer to raw medicinal materials formed after the medicinal parts of medicinal plants and animals are harvested and subjected to primary processing at the place of production." The document "Reply on Issues Concerning the Operation of Chinese Medicinal Materials in Urban and Rural Trade Markets" (State Food and Drug Administration [2006] No. 63) states: "According to the Quality Management Standard for the Production of Chinese Medicinal Materials, 'primary processing at the place of production of Chinese medicinal materials' mainly refers to appropriate processing such as sorting, washing, cutting, or trimming after harvesting, so that the Chinese medicinal materials are not contaminated and the active ingredients are not damaged." The product at issue involves grinding Cordyceps sinensis into powder and filling it into capsules, which clearly exceeds the scope of "primary processing at the place of production of Chinese medicinal materials" and should be regarded as the production and processing of Chinese medicinal materials. Article 100, paragraph 1 of the Drug Administration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Drugs refer to substances used for the prevention, treatment, and diagnosis of human diseases, and for the purposeful regulation of human physiological functions, with specified indications or functions, usage, and dosage, including Chinese medicinal materials, traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces, proprietary Chinese medicines, chemical raw drugs and their preparations, antibiotics, biochemical drugs, radioactive drugs, sera, vaccines, blood products, and diagnostic drugs." Articles 7 and 14 of the Drug Administration Law respectively provide that the production and operation of drugs are subject to the drug manufacturing license system and the drug operation license system. However, Article 21, paragraph 1 of the Drug Administration Law provides: "Urban and rural trade markets may sell Chinese medicinal materials, except as otherwise provided by the State Council." Article 31, paragraph 1 of the Drug Administration Law provides: "The production of new drugs or drugs with existing national standards shall be approved by the drug regulatory authority of the State Council, which shall issue an approval document number; however, the production of Chinese medicinal materials and traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces that are not subject to approval document number management is excluded. The catalogue of Chinese medicinal materials and traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces subject to approval document number management shall be formulated by the drug regulatory authority of the State Council jointly with the traditional Chinese medicine regulatory authority of the State Council." Article 34 of the Drug Administration Law provides: "Drug manufacturers, drug distributors, and medical institutions must purchase drugs from enterprises that have the qualifications for drug production and operation; however, the purchase of Chinese medicinal materials that are not subject to approval document number management is excluded." Reading the above provisions together, Chinese medicinal materials are drugs, and the production and operation of drugs are generally subject to a licensing system. However, except for Chinese medicinal materials subject to approval document number management, the production and operation of Chinese medicinal materials are not subject to a licensing system. Upon inquiry into the "catalogue of Chinese medicinal materials and traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces subject to approval document number management" formulated by the drug regulatory authority of the State Council jointly with the traditional Chinese medicine regulatory authority of the State Council, Cordyceps sinensis is not subject to approval document number management, and therefore its production and operation do not require a license. Article 16 of the Chongqing Product Quality Regulations provides: "Producers, sellers, and service operators shall not engage in the following acts: (1) Using marks and numbers of production licenses for products that are not subject to the production license system; ..." The product at issue, being a product not subject to the production license system, clearly violated this provision by using a production license number.

II. Whether the merchant constitutes fraud.

The act of labeling a drug manufacturing license number on the product at issue violates the Chongqing Product Quality Regulations. However, whether this act constitutes fraud must be comprehensively determined by combining the provisions on fraud under the Consumer Rights Protection Law, relevant civil law principles, and the facts of the case. First, the drug manufacturing license number indicated on the product at issue was legally obtained by Huiyuan Company from the relevant state authority. Since the number corresponds to a specific product scope, it should not have been labeled on the product at issue. However, because the number itself was lawfully obtained by the enterprise, it does not constitute fraudulent use. Second, since the drug manufacturing license number itself does not display its corresponding scope of production, it cannot be determined that the appellant Chen Xueqin, relying on the drug manufacturing license number, purchased the product as a traditional Chinese medicine decoction piece, and thus fraud cannot be found. Third, considering the ordinary consumer's typical level of knowledge, labeling a drug manufacturing license number on the product at issue would likely have a significant impact on Chen Xueqin's decision to purchase the product as a drug. However, according to Article 100 of the Drug Administration Law, Chinese medicinal materials, traditional Chinese medicine decoction pieces, etc., are all drugs. Therefore, even if the improper labeling led Chen Xueqin to believe that the product at issue was a drug, such belief would not be a mistaken belief, and there is no fact that she was misled into a mistaken belief due to the other party's fraudulent conduct. Fourth, Chen Xueqin's agent stated in court that there was no clear purchase purpose; she bought it because she thought it was good. Therefore, while such improper labeling may strengthen a consumer's confidence to purchase, it is not the main reason for inducing the purchase intention. In summary, the labeling of a drug manufacturing license number on the product at issue cannot support a finding of fraud by the appellee Century Xindu.

Regarding whether the "false quality conformity mark" constitutes fraud: Article 6, paragraph 2 of the Standardization Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Where no national standards or industry standards exist for a product produced by an enterprise, the enterprise shall formulate an enterprise standard as a basis for organizing production. The enterprise's product standard must be filed with the local government standardization administrative department and the relevant competent administrative department." This provision indicates that where no national, industry, or local standards exist for the product at issue, it is not improper for the enterprise to formulate and implement an enterprise standard, but it must be filed with the local government standardization administrative department and the relevant competent administrative department. However, the enterprise standard implemented by the product at issue was not lawfully filed. Nevertheless, failure to file does not equate to the product being of non-conforming quality. There is no evidence that the product at issue is of non-conforming quality. Therefore, the mere fact that the enterprise self-labeled "quality qualified" cannot support a finding of fraud.

III. Liability.

The fact that the merchant does not constitute fraud does not mean it bears no civil liability. Product labeling is an important means for consumers to identify product performance, characteristics, and value, and an important source of information for consumers to make consumption choices. Producers and sellers shall ensure the truthfulness and accuracy of product labeling content. This is especially true for products like the one at issue, where ordinary consumers lack the ability to identify the nature of the raw material (Cordyceps sinensis). After grinding Cordyceps sinensis into powder and filling it into capsules, the appearance significantly changes, making it even more difficult for consumers to judge the nature of the product. In such circumstances, product labeling is even more important for consumers to understand the product and make purchase decisions consistent with their true intentions. The appellee Century Xindu, as a seller, has the duty to inspect the truthfulness and accuracy of product labeling. The product at issue is not subject to a licensing system, and its production and sale do not require a license. Therefore, Century Xindu did not need a drug operation license to sell the product. However, the outer packaging of the product at issue bore a drug manufacturing license number, and the product corresponding to that license number does not include the product at issue. Century Xindu should be deemed to have "knowingly" sold the product with improper labeling and shall bear corresponding liability.

Article 40 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Where a product sold falls under any of the following circumstances, the seller shall be liable for repair, replacement, or return; if losses are caused to the consumer who purchased the product, the seller shall compensate for such losses: ... (2) The product does not conform to the product standard indicated on the product or its packaging; ..." The product at issue is not subject to a licensing system but improperly bears a drug manufacturing license number, which is likely to cause consumers to confuse it with products subject to a licensing system, even though the management systems and quality standards applicable to the two are different. Moreover, the product at issue self-labels "product quality qualified" without having its enterprise standard filed, which also falls under non-standard product labeling. Thus, the product at issue falls within the situation of "not conforming to the product standard indicated on the product or its packaging." The appellee Century Xindu failed to fulfill its corresponding inspection and warranty obligations and, in accordance with Article 40, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Product Quality Law, shall be liable for return of the goods.

In summary, the act of the appellee Century Xindu in selling Cordyceps sinensis capsules labeled with a drug manufacturing license number violated Article 16 of the Chongqing Product Quality Regulations, but this act does not meet the constitutive elements of fraud. Therefore, the appellant Chen Xueqin's claim that the appellees New Century Department Store Company and Century Xindu constituted fraud, entitling her to triple damages, is not established. However, in accordance with Article 40 of the Product Quality Law, her claim for a refund of the purchase price is supported.

Accordingly, the Chongqing First Intermediate People's Court, in accordance with Article 40, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 170, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment on December 16, 2016:

1. Reversed the civil judgment (2015) Jiang Fa Min Chu Zi No. 07133 of the Jiangbei District People's Court of Chongqing;

2. The appellee Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd., Century Xindu Branch shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, refund to the appellant Chen Xueqin the purchase price of RMB 50,046. The appellee Chongqing Commercial Group New Century Department Store Chain Co., Ltd. shall bear supplementary liability for the portion of Century Xindu Branch's assets insufficient to satisfy the obligation;

3. Dismissed all other claims of the appellant Chen Xueqin.

This judgment is final.
